title: Macron Hosts Saudi Crown Prince for Talks on Energy and Conflict
summary:
French President Emmanuel Macron is hosting Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) for a two-day state visit in Paris, starting with the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup. This is the first time the competition, which spans video games to chess, has been held outside Saudi Arabia.

The visit includes bilateral meetings and a business forum on Monday. Macron's office said the leaders will discuss "the main topics of regional importance, within a framework of close collaboration between France and her partners in the Gulf." Key topics include energy routes that could bypass the Strait of Hormuz, the Iran conflict, Gaza-Israel, and developments in Lebanon and Syria.

Several agreements on health, transport, and energy are due to be signed. However, Macron's adviser noted that finding a resolution to the US-Israel war on Iran, now in its sixth month, remains out of reach, saying "It's difficult to see a way out."

This is MBS's third visit to Paris, following trips in 2022 and 2023. It comes after Saudi Arabia signed a trilateral defence pact with Turkiye and Pakistan on August 7, known as the Mecca pact. The pact commits all three states to treat an armed attack on any one as an attack on all three. Analysts say this reflects Riyadh's push to diversify security partnerships beyond Washington.

France has been a long-standing weapons supplier to Gulf states, and Saudi Arabia is positioning itself as a growing investor in the French economy. The two leaders last met in April in Islamabad, where they agreed to stay in "close contact" on de-escalation efforts.

Saudi Arabia is set to host Expo 2030 and the 2034 football World Cup, which will likely feature in discussions. This visit highlights the strengthening ties between France and Saudi Arabia amid shifting regional dynamics.
why_it_matters: This visit shows how diplomacy works through personal meetings, agreements, and symbolic events, even when war continues elsewhere. Understanding these relationships helps young people see how countries use both cooperation and rivalry to shape the world they live in.

background_read: Emmanuel Macron is the president of France, and Mohammed bin Salman is Saudi Arabia's crown prince and day-to-day leader.
A state visit is a formal, high-level trip to a foreign country, often involving ceremonies, meetings, and signed agreements.
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway in the Middle East that a huge share of the world's oil passes through, making it important to global energy security.
Saudi Arabia has been working to expand its partnerships beyond the United States, including a trilateral defence pact with Turkiye and Pakistan known as the Mecca pact.
France has been a long-standing weapons supplier to Gulf states, while Saudi Arabia is becoming a bigger investor in the French economy.

perspectives.description: For France and Saudi Arabia, the visit is an opportunity to sign real agreements on health, transport, and energy and to build business ties that benefit both economies. It gives Saudi Arabia influence in Europe and gives France access to a wealthy investment partner.

Critics may see the visit as giving international prestige to MBS despite serious concerns about Saudi Arabia's human-rights record. It also exposes the limits of diplomacy: Macron's adviser admitted there is no easy solution to the war with Iran, even after months of conflict.

This is a familiar pattern in international relations: countries with different political systems still trade, invest, and sign security agreements when it serves their interests. The Mecca pact suggests Gulf states are looking to reduce their dependence on the U.S., while France uses its ties to stay relevant in the Middle East.

If the talks succeed, France and Saudi Arabia could deepen cooperation on energy, defence, and major events like Expo 2030 and the 2034 World Cup. The challenge will be whether those partnerships also help de-escalate regional conflicts or simply reinforce the status quo.
